I don't see the threat here at all.

Monsanto is able to control a large fraction of the agriculture market because the GMO crops produce much higher yields than other strains. It's hard to compete against GMO corn if your regular corn costs significantly more per bushel.

But the marijuana market will never be like the corn market - the consumer buys the plant itself, not the things that are made from it. So long as there is demand for non-GMO marijuana, there are plenty of people who will be happy to grow it and sell it at a reasonable price.

Weed will be like beer once its legalized - you'll have mass-market stuff like Budweiser, and a million other choices from many smaller makers. Plus most of us will probably be growing our own anyway.

They won't get into it because it's a waste of time, money and resources to do so. I can easily plant 1000 seeds, find that one special plant that has all the qualities I want and have it fully stress tested in under a year and I'm just a home grower in a highly illegal market. You put someone like me in a fully funded legal setting and within a few years I could have lines that produce specific tastes, smells, cannabinoid ratios, etc. all in seed form that breed those traits dominantly into other varieties all without the use of any genetic modification at all. The problem really is that while you can make some classic strains that will stand the test of time they can easily be stolen from you if you sell any kind of plant material to the public and you can never keep up with the public's desire for something new. So yeah if they get into it it'll likely be for the medicinal side of things where quality control is expected and governments are likely to pony up the fees to professionals like monsanto to take care of everything for them but outside of those strictly controlled conditions I wouldn't expect the likes of monsanto or any other company like them to so much as look at us as a potential market.

Unfortunately, the document seems very disorganized.

Obviously it is not the actual document used internally by the Linux Foundation, because it tries to account for multiple distributions and security systems, whereas internal policy would, I imagine, prescribe only one distribution and specific configurations. Besides, it says so in the Readme.

But this isn't the problem. The problems are:

  1. It's a mix of recommendations for system administrators and users.
  2. It doesn't really distinguish between threats (local malicious users, malware, remote hackers, government agencies etc.).
  3. Too much stuff is listed as "CRITICAL". For example, SELinux. I've heard testimonies of admins who noted that SELinux may or may not prevent attacks (which may or may not happen), but the only thing that it will definitely do is make your life much more difficult.
